abstract: Background Oxidative stress damage is the important mechanism that promotes the process of fibrosis. Whether mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) regulate mitochondrial dynamics and oxidative stress via armadillo repeat containing 1 (ARMC1) in renal fibrosis? Methods Using proteomics analysis, compare the significant differences in renal tissue proteins before and after MSCs intervention in adenine-induced nephropathy. Using a lentiviral vector to overexpress the ARMC1 gene in HK-2 cells, with the empty vector as a control. MSCs conditioned media (MSCs-CM) was applied to TGF-β1 treated cells, and MSCs were used in a cisplatin-induced nephropathy mouse model to assess mitochondrial dynamics, ROS generation, antioxidant stress, and fibrosis indicators, with Mdivi-1 (a Drp1 inhibitor) and Apocynin (a selective NADPH oxidase inhibitor) as positive controls. Results Renal proteomics showed that MSCs increased ARMC1 protein in the renal tissue of adenine nephropathy (3.521 times). In vitro, MSCs-CM increased ARMC1, reduced DRP1, and enhanced OPA1 and MFN2, lowering ROS, boosting mitochondrial bioactivity, and increasing antioxidant proteins NRF2, SOD1, SOD2, and CAT while decreasing fibrosis markers α-SMA, FN, COL-I, and KIM-1, and raising E-cadherin. The indicator variations in ARMC1-OE cells and OE-Con cells were similar between subgroups; Notably, under identical treatment conditions, the shifts in indicators within ARMC1-OE cells were more significant than those observed in OE-Con cells. In cisplatin-induced nephropathy mice, MSCs, Apocynin, and Mdivi-1 improved renal function and reduced interstitial collagen deposition, inhibited mitochondrial fission, enhanced antioxidant capacity, and reduced fibrosis. However, individual interventions were found to be less effective than their combined counterparts, with the synergistic impact of MSCs and Mdivi-1 achieving the most remarkable outcomes. Conclusion MSCs have the potential to improve renal fibrosis by influencing mitochondrial dynamics and oxidative stress through the upregulation of ARMC1 expression. ARMC1 may be an effective target for anti-fibrosis. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s13287-025-04706-7.

Materials and methods
Isolation and culture of primary MSCs and preparation of MSCs conditioned media (MSCs-CM)
Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) derived from bone marrow were extracted from the femur and tibia of healthy male Sprague Dawley young rats (5–6 weeks, weighing 120–150 g), sourced from the Laboratory Animal Center at Southwest Medical University in Sichuan, China. Cells were cultivated in DMEM/F12 basic medium, supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 2.5 mM L-glutamine and penicillin/streptomycin within a 5% CO
2
incubator maintained at 37 °C. These reagents were mainly procured from Gibco brand, Invitrogen, USA. Cells were passaged to the third generation at a fixed ratio of 1:3. When reaching 90% confluence, a 0.25% trypsin-EDTA solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) was used to digest the cells for phenotypic validation. The characterization of bone marrow-derived MSCs has been validated in our previous studies [
13
]. The flow cytometry detection of cell surface markers and their trilineage differentiation potential into osteoblasts, chondrocytes, and adipocytes was not validated for reproducibility in this study.
After being passaged to the second generation, MSCs were cryopreserved in liquid nitrogen for future experiments. Prior to initiating cell experiments, the cells were retrieved from liquid nitrogen and thawed. To maintain the high biological activity of MSCs, they were initially cultured in DMEM/F12 complete medium containing 15% FBS. When MSCs reached about 80% confluence, discarded the old culture medium, then added fresh prepared complete medium containing 10% FBS, and continued to culture for 24 h. The supernatant was collected and filtered through a 0.22 μm sterile filter membrane to remove cell debris, resulting in MSCs-conditioned medium (MSCs-CM). To ensure the efficacy of the cytokines, MSCs-CM was stored in small aliquots at -80 °C and used within two months. To eliminate serum interference, the supernatant of normal HK-2 cultured with the same concentration of serum for the same duration was used as a control, collected and processed in the same way as MSCs-CM.
Adenine-induced rat nephropathy and administration of MSCs
Male Sprague Dawley rats (8–12 w,
n

The rats were maintained in specific pathogen-free environments at 24 °C with 50% relative humidity, following a 12-hour light/dark cycle. They were randomly allocated into three groups based on a random number table: Control group (Control), Adenine-induced nephropathy group (Adenine), and MSCs treatment group (Adenine + MSCs) (
n

n

Adenine was continued after a 2-day pause on the 10th day of gavage. The adenine + MSCs group received an injection of 1 mL of MSCs suspension (2.0 × 10
6
MSCs/kg) via the tail vein on the third day after modeling. In contrast, the control group was administered an equivalent volume of saline. After 5 days of MSCs treatment, serum creatinine and urea nitrogen levels were determined with a kit from AmyJet Scientific Inc (Wuhan, Hubei, China). Measurements of serum creatinine and urea nitrogen were conducted utilizing a Beckman Analyzer II (Beckman Instruments, Inc. USA). All animal experiments were sanctioned by the Southwest Medical University Animal Experimentation Ethics Committee and were executed in compliance with the endorsed guidelines (SWMU201803147). The work has been reported in line with the ARRIVE guidelines 2.0._Adenine.
Pathological and immunohistochemical staining of rat kidneys
The kidneys were preserved in a phosphate buffer solution (PBS) containing 4% paraformaldehyde before being embedded in paraffin. Tissue section (5 μm) were stained using Hematoxylin-Eosin, Masson (Solarbio, Beijing, China), and Sirus Red staining (Yeasen Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) according to the specified protocols and examined under a microscope. The kidney index was calculated using the formula: (the mass of both kidneys / the body weight of the mouse) × 100%. Semi-quantitative analysis of collagen deposition in renal tissue by Masson and Sirus Red staining was quantified in 6 cortical high-power fields (HPFs) per rat using ImageJ Software.
For immunohistochemical staining, tissue sections were treated with 3% H
2
O
2
in PBS for 15 min to block endogenous peroxidase activity. Subsequently, nonspecific binding sites were inhibited using 5% goat serum for 30 min at room temperature. The slices were then incubated overnight at 4 °C with the following primary antibodies: rabbit anti-α-SMA antibody (Abcam, UK) diluted 1:100 and rabbit collagen I (Abcam, UK) diluted 1:50. Following this, an HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody (Abcam, UK) was applied and incubated for 1.5 h at room temperature. After washing with PBS, use 3,3’-diaminobenzidine (DAB) for coloration, followed by gradient ethanol dehydration, xylene clearing, neutral gum mounting, and observation under an optical microscope. Semi-quantitative analysis of positive staining integrated optical density (IOD) was performed using ImageJ software in six comparable high magnification fields (200×), with the ratio to the average IOD of the control group representing the relative expression level.

Protein digestion was executed following the filter-aided sample preparation method delineated by Wisniewski [
14
], with the resultant peptide mixture labeled using the 8-plex iTRAQ reagent in accordance with the manufacturer’s guidelines (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA). In brief, 30 µL of protein digestion for each sample was combined with dithiothreitol (DTT) to reach a final concentration of 100 mM, boiled in water for 5 min, and then allowed to cool to room temperature. The detergent, DTT, and other low-molecular-weight constituents were eliminated by repeated ultrafiltration using 200 µL UA Buffer (8 M Urea and 150 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0). Subsequently, 100 µL of IAA buffer (0.1 M iodoacetamide in UA Buffer) was introduced to inhibit cysteine residues, with samples incubated in darkness for 30 min. The filters underwent two washes with 100 µL UA buffer, followed by two additional washes with 100 µL dissolution buffer. Ultimately, the protein suspensions were digested overnight at 37℃ with 4 µg trypsin (Promega, Madison, WI) in 40 µL of dissolution, and the resulting peptides were collected as a filtrate. The peptide concentration was assessed by UV light spectral density at 280 nm using a Nano Drop 2000. From each sample, 100 µg of peptides were labeled according to the iTRAQ Reagent-8 plex Multiplex Kit (AB Sciex, UK). The peptides were then combined into a pool. This pooled mixture was subsequently divided equally into three fractions (Control group: A1 and A2; Adenine group: B1, B2, and B3; Adenine + MSCs group: C1, C2, and C3). An internal control was established using a standard pool consisting of equal amounts of protein from all samples. The samples were designated as A1-113, A2-114, B1-115, B2-116, B3-117, C1-118, C2-119, and C3-121, followed by multiplexing and vacuum drying. For labeling, each iTRAQ reagent was dissolved in 70 µL of ethanol and added to the corresponding peptide mixture. This experiment was conducted with three biological replicates.
All labeled samples were combined in equal proportions. Subsequently, these samples underwent fractionation utilizing an Agilent 1260 Infinity II high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system (Thermo Dinoex Ultimate 3000 BioRS) equipped with an XBridge Peptide BEH C18 (130Å, 5 μm, 4.6 mm × 100 mm) column. The LC-MS/MS analysis was conducted using a Q Exactive Plus LC-MS/MS system (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, Massachusetts, USA).
Bioinformatic analysis
The analysis focused on the differentially expressed proteins between the Adenine group and the Adenine + MSCs group based on the experimental objectives. The mass spectrometry data was meticulously evaluated utilizing Proteome Discoverer 2.1 (Thermo Scientific) and Mascot 2.5 software. Peptide identifications were executed through the Paragon algorithm, querying the uniprot Rattus Norvegicus protein database (
http://www.uniprot.org/
). Only peptides with a false discovery rate (FDR) value set below 0.01 were included in the iTRAQ labeling quantification, while proteins exhibiting an average fold change exceeding 1.2 were deemed significantly differentially expressed for further examination. To elucidate the biological and functional characteristics of the identified proteins, the sequences were mapped to Gene Ontology Terms (
http://geneontology.org/
). Initially, a homology search was conducted for all identified sequences using the localized NCBI BLAST+ (ncbi-blast-2.2.28+-win32.exe) program against the NCBI database. The e-value threshold was established at less than 0.001, and the most favorable hit for each query sequence was utilized for GO term matching. Information regarding molecular functions, cellular components, and biological processes was obtained through a search using relevant terms and gene products. GO term matching was facilitated by the Blast2go Command Line. When conducting cluster analysis, the quantitative information of the target protein set was first normalized (normalized to the range of (− 1,1)). Secondly, the Cluster 3.0 software was used to classify both the sample and protein expression levels simultaneously (distance algorithm: Euclidean, linkage method: Average linkage). Finally, the Java Trewview software was used to generate a hierarchical clustering heatmap. The raw data of proteomics was in the supplementary file of Renal Proteomics Raw Data.
Cell experiments
The effect of TGF-β1 on the expression of ARMC1 protein in HK-2 cells
To investigate the effects of TGF-β1 on ARMC1 protein, mitochondrial dynamics, oxidative stress resistance, and fibrosis, human renal proximal tubular epithelial cells (HK-2) were obtained from BNBIO in Beijing, China. Following standard thawing procedures, the cells were incubated at 37 °C in a 5% CO
2
environment for cultivation. The complete culture medium was prepared using 90% DMEM/F12 basal medium, 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), and 1% penicillin-streptomycin. Once the cells reached approximately 90% confluence, they were passaged at a ratio of 1:3 for further experiments. HK-2 cells were then treated with 10 ng/mL of human recombinant TGF-β1 protein (Proteintech, USA) for durations of 24, 48, and 72 h. Using Western blotting to assess the expression changes related to apoptosis (Bax, BCL-2), epithelial-mesenchymal transition (α-SMA, E-cadherin), kidney injury molecule (KIM-1), ARCM1, mitochondrial dynamics (DRP1, MFN2), and antioxidant stress capacity (Nrf2, SOD1, SOD2) proteins.
ROS detection
To evaluate the effect of MSCs-CM on ROS levels, HK-2 cells were plated at a density of 1.4 × 10
5
cells in 6-well plates and categorized into six groups: control, TGF-β1, TGF-β1 + MSCs-CM, TGF-β1 + DMEM/F12, MSCs-CM, and ROSUP as positive control. The TGF-β1 group treated the cells with 10 ng/mL TGF-β1 for 48 h. Then, the TGF-β1 + MSCs-CM and TGF-β1 + DMEM/F12 groups removed the old culture medium and added an equal volume of MSCs-CM and DMEM/F12 supernatant that had been thawed in advance from the same batch, continuing the treatment for another 48 h. The MSCs-CM group received direct treatment with the same batch of fresh thawed MSCs-CM. The ROSUP group utilized the recommended diluted ROSUP for pre-stimulation. To detect ROS levels, the DCFH-DA probe was loaded according to the ROS Assay Kit instructions (Beyotime, China). Under a 100× microscope, five different fields of fluorescent images were collected, and their grayscale values were analyzed using ImageJ software.

15
]. HK-2 cells were rich in NOX4 [
16
], we used the selective NOX4 inhibitor Apocynin as a positive control. To compare the effects of MSCs-CM and Apocynin on ROS production, HK-2 cells (7 × 10
4
/well) were seeded in 24-well plates. Simultaneously, HK-2 cells (5,000/well) were seeded in 96-well plates, and CCK8 was used to detect the effect of different concentrations of Apocynin on cell viability. To compare the differences in ROS generation and the expression of the endogenous antioxidant stress signal nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) and the antioxidant enzyme CAT protein between MSCs-CM and Apocynin, HK-2 cells were seeded in 24-well plates (7 × 10
4
/well) or cell culture dishes (1.5 × 10
5
/well), and divided into 8 groups: Con, TGF-β1, TGF-β1 + MSCs-CM, TGF-β1 + Apocynin, TGF-β1 + MSCs-CM + Apocynin, MSCs-CM, Apocynin, and MSCs-CM + Apocynin. After TGF-β1 treatment, Apocynin (200 µM) or MSCs-CM or both were continued to treat the cells for 24 h. Cell samples were collected and proteins were extracted, and western blot was used to detect the expression of NRF2 and CAT proteins.
Mitochondrial biological activity assays
To observe the effect of MSCs-CM on the mitochondrial bioactivity of HK-2 cells, equal amounts of HK-2 cells were seeded in a 6-well plate, grouped, and treated similarly to the ROS detection without a positive control. Mitochondrial fluorescent probes were loaded following the Mito-Tracker Red CMXRos detection kit instructions (Beyotime, China). Under a 200× microscope, five different fields of fluorescent images were collected, and their grayscale values were analyzed using ImageJ software.
To preliminarily observe the effects of MSCs-CM on ARMC1 and oxidative stress resistance in the TGF-β1 induced HK-2 fibrosis model, the protein expression of ARMC1, mitochondrial fission protein (DRP1), and antioxidant stress capacity (Nrf2 and CAT) was detected by Western blot.
Construction of lentiviral vectors for ARMC1 gene regulation cells
To study the role of ARMC1 gene regulation in the antifibrotic process of MSCs, we utilized lentiviral vectors (Genechem, Shanghai, China) to knockdown and overexpress the Armc1 gene (ARMC1-KD and ARMC1-OE) in HK-2 cells, with an empty vector as controls (KD-Con and OE-Con). Western blot confirmed the expression of Armc1 protein. After the antibiotic screening, the four cell lines KD-Con, OE-Con, ARMC1-KD, and ARMC1-OE were continuously cultured under normal culture conditions for 24, 48, and 72 h, followed by CCK8 assay to detect cell viability.
Mitochondrial dynamics and oxidative stress resistance detection
Under the condition of ARMC1-OE, in order to study the effects of MSCs-CM on mitochondrial dynamics, biological activity, and antioxidant stress capacity of HK-2 cells treated with TGF-β1, cells were divided into two primary groups: the OE-Con group and the ARMC1-OE group. Each group was further divided into five subgroups, and the grouping and treatment of all subgroups were the same as the mitochondrial bioactivity detection. The protein expression of mitochondrial dynamics (ARMC1, DRP1, MFN1, MFN2, OPA1), oxidative stress resistance (NRF2, SOD1, SOD2, CAT), and fibrosis (α-SMA, FN, KIM-1) was detected by Western blot. Similarly, Mito-Tracker Red CMXRos was used to assess the mitochondrial bioactivity of cells in each group.
Cisplatin-induced renal interstitial fibrosis in mice, grouping and treatment
Cisplatin was a widely used chemotherapy drug with nephrotoxicity. Cisplatin caused an imbalance in the intracellular redox state, resulting in excessive ROS [
15
]. Both cisplatin and TGF-β1 can promote p53 phosphorylation and subsequent tubular dysfunction through NOXs-mediated ROS production [
17
]. Therefore, oxidative stress is one of the key factors promoting the process of renal fibrosis [
18
]. The kidneys are one of the organs with high oxygen consumption and are rich in mitochondria, especially in proximal tubular epithelial cells. The mechanism of adenine-induced renal fibrosis was that excessive adenine can be converted into adenosine monophosphate and adenosine triphosphate in the body, leading to the accumulation of metabolic alterations in the renal tubules, which may cause cytotoxicity, resulting in damage and death of renal tubular epithelial cells, as well as local inflammatory responses, affecting normal renal function [
19
]. So, the cisplatin-induced mouse model has become a classic model for studying the oxidative stress damage and fibrosis. Although the two modeling methods were different, both primarily exhibited renal interstitial fibrosis as the main pathological manifestation.
To observe whether the ARMC1 gene increases the anti-oxidative stress capacity to improve fibrosis by regulating dynamics in the MSCs anti-cisplatin induced renal interstitial fibrosis model, we chose male C57BL/6J mice as the research subjects. A total of 70 male C57BL/6J mice, aged 6 to 8 weeks (weight 20–30 g), were obtained from the Experimental Animal Center of Southwest Medical University. The mice were maintained in a controlled environment at 24 °C and 50% relative humidity, following a 12-hour light/dark cycle. They underwent various experiments in a specific pathogen-free (SPF) laboratory within the center. Throughout the study, all procedures complied with relevant animal ethics laws and regulations. The experiment received approval from Southwest Medical University, under the animal ethics number SWMU20240014. The work has been reported in line with the ARRIVE guidelines 2.0_Cisplatin.
C57BL/6J mice were randomly assigned to seven groups: the Control, the Cisplatin, the Cisplatin + MSCs group, the Cisplatin + Apocynin group, the C group, the Cisplatin + MSCs + Apocynin group, and the Cisplatin + MSCs + Mdivi-1 group, 10 mice per group. Mdivi-1(MCE, Shanghai, Chian) is a selective inhibitor of Drp1, which can effectively block the processes of mitochondrial fission and mitophagy, serving as a control for the effects on mitochondrial dynamics during the anti-cisplatin-induced fibrosis process of MSCs. Apocynin (MCE, Shanghai, China) is a selective NADPH oxidase inhibitor, used as a control against the oxidative stress damage. Mice were injected intraperitoneally with a saline solution of cisplatin at a concentration of 1 mg/mL (7 mg/kg) once a week for four consecutive weeks to create a model of cisplatin-induced nephropathy. Starting from the fifth week, the Cisplatin + Mdivi-1 group, Cisplatin + Apocynin group, Cisplatin + MSCs + Mdivi-1 group, and Cisplatin + MSCs + Apocynin group received Mdivi-1 or Apocynin intervention, with a concentration of 1 mg/mL and a standard of 10 mg/kg, administered by intraperitoneal injection once a day for 7 consecutive days. Simultaneously, the MSCs group, MSCs + Mdivi-1 group, and MSCs + Apocynin group received a tail vein injection of a cell density of 1 × 10
6
/mL MSCs suspension (1 × 10
7
/kg). The control group was given an equivalent volume of solvent. To adhere to animal ethics principles and ensure the welfare of the mice at the end of the experiment, we first anesthetized them intraperitoneally with a 1% pentobarbital sodium (50 mg/kg) and then performed euthanasia through cervical dislocation, ensuring that the mice ended their lives without pain at the conclusion of the sixth week. And then, the kidneys were harvested and weighed, and cardiac blood samples were collected.
Mouse kidney function testing
All mice were fasted the night before blood collection. Mice were anesthetized intraperitoneally with 1% pentobarbital sodium, and cardiac blood samples were collected via thoracotomy. Subsequently, serum was collected by centrifugation at 3500 rpm for 15 min to assess renal function indicators, specifically blood urea nitrogen and creatinine. The serum creatinine levels were determined using the creatinine oxidase method, while the serum urea nitrogen levels were assessed using the urease method according to the instructions of the test kit (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, Nanjing, China). Additionally, the kidney index was calculated using the formula: kidney weight divided by mouse weight, multiplied by 100%.
Mouse kidney pathological staining
The kidney tissue was fixed using 4% paraformaldehyde, followed by gradient alcohol dehydration, xylene infiltration, and then embedded in paraffin before sectioning to a thickness of 5 μm. For all groups, the kidney tissues underwent a standard process of xylene deparaffinization and gradient alcohol hydration. Subsequently, the sections were stained using Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE), Masson, and Red Sirius according to the reagent kit (Solarbio Biological Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). Once the staining was completed, images were captured using a light microscope. The tubular injury score was mainly based on the degree and extent of tubular injury, changes in renal tubular epithelial cell morphology, alterations in tubular lumen, and interstitial inflammation [
20
,
21
]. For each mouse, four to six high-power fields (HPF, 200×) of the same level were selected to assess collagen deposition and the integrated optical densities of immunohistochemically labeled collagen I and α-SMA. This evaluation was conducted semi-quantitatively using Image Pro Plus version 6.0 software (Media Cybernetics, Silver Spring, USA).
Western blot
The samples of cells were lysed on ice using RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with 1 mM PMSF (Beyotime, China), and the protein concentration was measured with a BCA kit (Beyotime, China). For kidney tissues, approximately 100 mg of tissue was collected and subsequently homogenized into a fine powder utilizing liquid nitrogen. The powder was subsequently transferred into a 1.5 mL tube, where 500 µL of RIPA lysis buffer was incorporated to promote effective lysis, while maintaining the mixture on ice to preserve protein integrity. Upon completion of the lysis procedure, the mixture was subjected to centrifugation at a velocity of 10, 000 rpm for a duration of 15 min at a temperature of 4 °C. Following centrifugation, the supernatant was extracted, and the protein concentration was also quantified using a BCA assay kit. For protein separation, 25–30 µg of protein was loaded onto an 8.0-12.5% SDS-PAGE gel, followed by transferring the proteins to a 0.45–0.22 μm PVDF membrane (Millipore, USA). After blocking the membrane with 5% skim milk, the following antibodies were incubated overnight at 4 °C: α-SMA (1:5000, Proteintech, USA), E-Cadherin (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), Collagen Type I (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), Fibronectin (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), KIM-1 (1:1000, SAB, USA), Bax (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), Bcl-2 (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), ARMC1 (1:1000, Invitrogen, USA), MFN1 (1:2000, Proteintech, USA), MFN2 (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), DRP1 (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), OPA1 (1:1000, Abcam, UK), NRF2 (1:2000, Abcam, UK), SOD1 (1:1000, Abcam, UK), SOD2 (1:1000, Abcam, UK), and CAT (1:1000, Abcam, UK). The PVDF membrane was then incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP) conjugated goat anti-rabbit or mouse secondary antibody for 2 h, followed by three washes with Tris Buffered Saline with Tween 20 (TBST). Afterward, the membrane was treated with a chemiluminescent HRP substrate (Beyotime, China), and the protein bands were visualized using the SH-Compact523 imaging system (Shenhua Technology, Hangzhou, China). Finally, the protein bands were quantified using Gel-Pro Analyzer software.
Statistical methods
In this study, all experimental results were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) derived from a minimum of three biological replicates. Statistical analyses were conducted utilizing GraphPad Prism 9.0 software (San Diego, CA, USA). To assess group differences, one-way ANOVA or two-way ANOVA was applied, accompanied by Tukey post hoc tests. A p-value less than 0.05 was considered to indicate a significant statistical difference.

After the antibiotic screening, the four cell lines KD-Con, OE-Con, ARMC1-KD, and ARMC1-OE were continuously cultured under normal culture conditions for 24, 48, and 72 h, followed by CCK8 assay to detect cell viability.
Mitochondrial dynamics and oxidative stress resistance detection
Under the condition of ARMC1-OE, in order to study the effects of MSCs-CM on mitochondrial dynamics, biological activity, and antioxidant stress capacity of HK-2 cells treated with TGF-β1, cells were divided into two primary groups: the OE-Con group and the ARMC1-OE group. Each group was further divided into five subgroups, and the grouping and treatment of all subgroups were the same as the mitochondrial bioactivity detection. The protein expression of mitochondrial dynamics (ARMC1, DRP1, MFN1, MFN2, OPA1), oxidative stress resistance (NRF2, SOD1, SOD2, CAT), and fibrosis (α-SMA, FN, KIM-1) was detected by Western blot. Similarly, Mito-Tracker Red CMXRos was used to assess the mitochondrial bioactivity of cells in each group.

Statistical methods
In this study, all experimental results were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) derived from a minimum of three biological replicates. Statistical analyses were conducted utilizing GraphPad Prism 9.0 software (San Diego, CA, USA). To assess group differences, one-way ANOVA or two-way ANOVA was applied, accompanied by Tukey post hoc tests. A p-value less than 0.05 was considered to indicate a significant statistical difference.

Introduction
Renal fibrosis is a prevalent pathological feature observed in various chronic kidney diseases (CKD) and acute kidney injury (AKI), representing a significant challenge and focus of research in this field. The primary pathological characteristics of renal fibrosis include abnormal deposition of the extracellular matrix, infiltration of inflammatory cells, thickening of the vascular endothelium, narrowing of the lumen, and a decline in renal function, which can ultimately lead to end-stage renal disease (ESRD) [
1
]. Mitochondria, known as the main sites for cellular energy production, play a crucial and multifaceted role in the development of renal fibrosis. They affect the pathological processes in the kidneys through several mechanisms, including the regulation of energy metabolism, oxidative stress, cell death, and signal transduction [
2
]. Mitochondria are also the primary source of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which contribute to inflammation and oxidative stress—both of which are key factors in the pathological progression of fibrosis [
3
]. ROS can result in cell damage and apoptosis, heighten inflammatory responses, and promote the release of fibrosis-related factors such as TGF-β1. These factors, in turn, stimulate the proliferation of fibroblasts and the synthesis of collagen [
4
]. Targeting mitochondrial regulation has emerged as a vital research direction in the study of antifibrotic therapies.
Numerous studies have proved that MSCs themselves or their derivatives have significant potential in delaying organ fibrosis, making MSCs one of the most promising options in antifibrotic therapy [
5
–
7
]. MSCs are advantageous due to their diverse sources, easy accessibility, ability to secrete multiple cytokines, and their properties that promote immune regulation, angiogenesis, and anti-inflammatory responses, all while maintaining a high safety profile [
8
,
9
]. In the adenine-induced rat renal fibrosis model, renal proteomics analysis showed that MSCs intervention significantly increased ARMC1 protein expression [
10
]. However, the specific role of ARMC1 in the context of MSCs’ anti-renal fibrosis effects remains unclear and necessitates further exploration.
ARMC1 is part of the ARMC family, which includes ARMC1-10, ARMC12, and ARMCX1 to 6. Members of this family are found across eukaryotic organisms and perform a variety of biological functions, such as transducing signals within cells, regulating mitochondrial functions, and influencing tumor development. The proteins produced by the ARMC family share a common domain, primarily consisting of a chain of 42 amino acids, which is crucial for interactions with other proteins and may significantly impact the development and treatment of various diseases [
11
]. In mammals, ARMC1 serves as a subunit of the mitochondrial contact site and cristae organizing system, also known as the mitochondrial intermembrane space bridging complex (MICOS/MIB), and is located in both the cytoplasm and mitochondria. It interacts with the outer mitochondrial membrane via its carboxy-terminal armadillo repeat domain and members of the solute carrier family. Notably, when ARMC1 is knocked out, mitochondria do not exhibit defects in crown structure, respiration, or protein content; however, they do show fragmentation and decreased motility [
12
]. This suggests that ARMC1 may play a role in regulating mitochondrial fission and fusion processes and/or in interactions with the cytoskeleton. According to the GeneCards database, ARMC1 is involved in regulating mitochondrial dynamics, which affects mitochondrial length, distribution, and motility. However, it remains uncertain whether MSCs utilize the ARMC1 gene to regulate mitochondrial dynamics and oxidative stress in order to combat renal fibrosis. This study aims to provide a foundational understanding of the antifibrotic mechanisms associated with MSCs.
Materials and methods
Isolation and culture of primary MSCs and preparation of MSCs conditioned media (MSCs-CM)
Mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) derived from bone marrow were extracted from the femur and tibia of healthy male Sprague Dawley young rats (5–6 weeks, weighing 120–150 g), sourced from the Laboratory Animal Center at Southwest Medical University in Sichuan, China. Cells were cultivated in DMEM/F12 basic medium, supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), 2.5 mM L-glutamine and penicillin/streptomycin within a 5% CO
2
incubator maintained at 37 °C. These reagents were mainly procured from Gibco brand, Invitrogen, USA. Cells were passaged to the third generation at a fixed ratio of 1:3. When reaching 90% confluence, a 0.25% trypsin-EDTA solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) was used to digest the cells for phenotypic validation. The characterization of bone marrow-derived MSCs has been validated in our previous studies [
13
]. The flow cytometry detection of cell surface markers and their trilineage differentiation potential into osteoblasts, chondrocytes, and adipocytes was not validated for reproducibility in this study.
After being passaged to the second generation, MSCs were cryopreserved in liquid nitrogen for future experiments. Prior to initiating cell experiments, the cells were retrieved from liquid nitrogen and thawed. To maintain the high biological activity of MSCs, they were initially cultured in DMEM/F12 complete medium containing 15% FBS. When MSCs reached about 80% confluence, discarded the old culture medium, then added fresh prepared complete medium containing 10% FBS, and continued to culture for 24 h. The supernatant was collected and filtered through a 0.22 μm sterile filter membrane to remove cell debris, resulting in MSCs-conditioned medium (MSCs-CM). To ensure the efficacy of the cytokines, MSCs-CM was stored in small aliquots at -80 °C and used within two months. To eliminate serum interference, the supernatant of normal HK-2 cultured with the same concentration of serum for the same duration was used as a control, collected and processed in the same way as MSCs-CM.
Adenine-induced rat nephropathy and administration of MSCs
Male Sprague Dawley rats (8–12 w,
n
= 40) were acquired from Dashuo Biotechnology Co. LTD (Chengdu, China). The rats were maintained in specific pathogen-free environments at 24 °C with 50% relative humidity, following a 12-hour light/dark cycle. They were randomly allocated into three groups based on a random number table: Control group (Control), Adenine-induced nephropathy group (Adenine), and MSCs treatment group (Adenine + MSCs) (
n
= 10 in Control group,
n
= 15 in Adenine group, and Adenine + MSCs group). The adenine group was induced via intragastric administration of 150 mg/kg adenine (Sigma Aldrich, USA) for a duration of 20 days. Adenine was continued after a 2-day pause on the 10th day of gavage. The adenine + MSCs group received an injection of 1 mL of MSCs suspension (2.0 × 10
6
MSCs/kg) via the tail vein on the third day after modeling. In contrast, the control group was administered an equivalent volume of saline. After 5 days of MSCs treatment, serum creatinine and urea nitrogen levels were determined with a kit from AmyJet Scientific Inc (Wuhan, Hubei, China). Measurements of serum creatinine and urea nitrogen were conducted utilizing a Beckman Analyzer II (Beckman Instruments, Inc. USA). All animal experiments were sanctioned by the Southwest Medical University Animal Experimentation Ethics Committee and were executed in compliance with the endorsed guidelines (SWMU201803147). The work has been reported in line with the ARRIVE guidelines 2.0._Adenine.
Pathological and immunohistochemical staining of rat kidneys
The kidneys were preserved in a phosphate buffer solution (PBS) containing 4% paraformaldehyde before being embedded in paraffin. Tissue section (5 μm) were stained using Hematoxylin-Eosin, Masson (Solarbio, Beijing, China), and Sirus Red staining (Yeasen Biotechnology, Shanghai, China) according to the specified protocols and examined under a microscope. The kidney index was calculated using the formula: (the mass of both kidneys / the body weight of the mouse) × 100%. Semi-quantitative analysis of collagen deposition in renal tissue by Masson and Sirus Red staining was quantified in 6 cortical high-power fields (HPFs) per rat using ImageJ Software.
For immunohistochemical staining, tissue sections were treated with 3% H
2
O
2
in PBS for 15 min to block endogenous peroxidase activity. Subsequently, nonspecific binding sites were inhibited using 5% goat serum for 30 min at room temperature. The slices were then incubated overnight at 4 °C with the following primary antibodies: rabbit anti-α-SMA antibody (Abcam, UK) diluted 1:100 and rabbit collagen I (Abcam, UK) diluted 1:50. Following this, an HRP-conjugated goat anti-rabbit IgG secondary antibody (Abcam, UK) was applied and incubated for 1.5 h at room temperature. After washing with PBS, use 3,3’-diaminobenzidine (DAB) for coloration, followed by gradient ethanol dehydration, xylene clearing, neutral gum mounting, and observation under an optical microscope. Semi-quantitative analysis of positive staining integrated optical density (IOD) was performed using ImageJ software in six comparable high magnification fields (200×), with the ratio to the average IOD of the control group representing the relative expression level.
Proteomics of rat kidney tissue
Sample processing, labeling, and mass spectrometry analysis
Rats were euthanized on Day 5 post-MSC intervention for renal proteomic analysis utilizing isobaric tags for relative and absolute quantification (iTRAQ). The study’s workflow was delineated in Supplement Fig.

Following ultrasonication, the homogenate was heated in boiling water for 15 min. The crude extract was then centrifuged at 14,000×

Protein digestion was executed following the filter-aided sample preparation method delineated by Wisniewski [
14
], with the resultant peptide mixture labeled using the 8-plex iTRAQ reagent in accordance with the manufacturer’s guidelines (Applied Biosystems, Foster City, CA). In brief, 30 µL of protein digestion for each sample was combined with dithiothreitol (DTT) to reach a final concentration of 100 mM, boiled in water for 5 min, and then allowed to cool to room temperature. The detergent, DTT, and other low-molecular-weight constituents were eliminated by repeated ultrafiltration using 200 µL UA Buffer (8 M Urea and 150 mM Tris-HCl, pH 8.0). Subsequently, 100 µL of IAA buffer (0.1 M iodoacetamide in UA Buffer) was introduced to inhibit cysteine residues, with samples incubated in darkness for 30 min. The filters underwent two washes with 100 µL UA buffer, followed by two additional washes with 100 µL dissolution buffer. Ultimately, the protein suspensions were digested overnight at 37℃ with 4 µg trypsin (Promega, Madison, WI) in 40 µL of dissolution, and the resulting peptides were collected as a filtrate. The peptide concentration was assessed by UV light spectral density at 280 nm using a Nano Drop 2000. From each sample, 100 µg of peptides were labeled according to the iTRAQ Reagent-8 plex Multiplex Kit (AB Sciex, UK). The peptides were then combined into a pool. This pooled mixture was subsequently divided equally into three fractions (Control group: A1 and A2; Adenine group: B1, B2, and B3; Adenine + MSCs group: C1, C2, and C3). An internal control was established using a standard pool consisting of equal amounts of protein from all samples. The samples were designated as A1-113, A2-114, B1-115, B2-116, B3-117, C1-118, C2-119, and C3-121, followed by multiplexing and vacuum drying. For labeling, each iTRAQ reagent was dissolved in 70 µL of ethanol and added to the corresponding peptide mixture. This experiment was conducted with three biological replicates.
All labeled samples were combined in equal proportions. Subsequently, these samples underwent fractionation utilizing an Agilent 1260 Infinity II high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) system (Thermo Dinoex Ultimate 3000 BioRS) equipped with an XBridge Peptide BEH C18 (130Å, 5 μm, 4.6 mm × 100 mm) column. The LC-MS/MS analysis was conducted using a Q Exactive Plus LC-MS/MS system (Thermo Scientific, Waltham, Massachusetts, USA).
Bioinformatic analysis
The analysis focused on the differentially expressed proteins between the Adenine group and the Adenine + MSCs group based on the experimental objectives. The mass spectrometry data was meticulously evaluated utilizing Proteome Discoverer 2.1 (Thermo Scientific) and Mascot 2.5 software. Peptide identifications were executed through the Paragon algorithm, querying the uniprot Rattus Norvegicus protein database (
http://www.uniprot.org/
). Only peptides with a false discovery rate (FDR) value set below 0.01 were included in the iTRAQ labeling quantification, while proteins exhibiting an average fold change exceeding 1.2 were deemed significantly differentially expressed for further examination. To elucidate the biological and functional characteristics of the identified proteins, the sequences were mapped to Gene Ontology Terms (
http://geneontology.org/
). Initially, a homology search was conducted for all identified sequences using the localized NCBI BLAST+ (ncbi-blast-2.2.28+-win32.exe) program against the NCBI database. The e-value threshold was established at less than 0.001, and the most favorable hit for each query sequence was utilized for GO term matching. Information regarding molecular functions, cellular components, and biological processes was obtained through a search using relevant terms and gene products. GO term matching was facilitated by the Blast2go Command Line. When conducting cluster analysis, the quantitative information of the target protein set was first normalized (normalized to the range of (− 1,1)). Secondly, the Cluster 3.0 software was used to classify both the sample and protein expression levels simultaneously (distance algorithm: Euclidean, linkage method: Average linkage). Finally, the Java Trewview software was used to generate a hierarchical clustering heatmap. The raw data of proteomics was in the supplementary file of Renal Proteomics Raw Data.
Cell experiments
The effect of TGF-β1 on the expression of ARMC1 protein in HK-2 cells
To investigate the effects of TGF-β1 on ARMC1 protein, mitochondrial dynamics, oxidative stress resistance, and fibrosis, human renal proximal tubular epithelial cells (HK-2) were obtained from BNBIO in Beijing, China. Following standard thawing procedures, the cells were incubated at 37 °C in a 5% CO
2
environment for cultivation. The complete culture medium was prepared using 90% DMEM/F12 basal medium, 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS), and 1% penicillin-streptomycin. Once the cells reached approximately 90% confluence, they were passaged at a ratio of 1:3 for further experiments. HK-2 cells were then treated with 10 ng/mL of human recombinant TGF-β1 protein (Proteintech, USA) for durations of 24, 48, and 72 h. Using Western blotting to assess the expression changes related to apoptosis (Bax, BCL-2), epithelial-mesenchymal transition (α-SMA, E-cadherin), kidney injury molecule (KIM-1), ARCM1, mitochondrial dynamics (DRP1, MFN2), and antioxidant stress capacity (Nrf2, SOD1, SOD2) proteins.
ROS detection
To evaluate the effect of MSCs-CM on ROS levels, HK-2 cells were plated at a density of 1.4 × 10
5
cells in 6-well plates and categorized into six groups: control, TGF-β1, TGF-β1 + MSCs-CM, TGF-β1 + DMEM/F12, MSCs-CM, and ROSUP as positive control. The TGF-β1 group treated the cells with 10 ng/mL TGF-β1 for 48 h. Then, the TGF-β1 + MSCs-CM and TGF-β1 + DMEM/F12 groups removed the old culture medium and added an equal volume of MSCs-CM and DMEM/F12 supernatant that had been thawed in advance from the same batch, continuing the treatment for another 48 h. The MSCs-CM group received direct treatment with the same batch of fresh thawed MSCs-CM. The ROSUP group utilized the recommended diluted ROSUP for pre-stimulation. To detect ROS levels, the DCFH-DA probe was loaded according to the ROS Assay Kit instructions (Beyotime, China). Under a 100× microscope, five different fields of fluorescent images were collected, and their grayscale values were analyzed using ImageJ software.
In HK-2 cells, ROS were generated not only due to mitochondrial damage but also from the activation of NADPH oxidases [
15
]. HK-2 cells were rich in NOX4 [
16
], we used the selective NOX4 inhibitor Apocynin as a positive control. To compare the effects of MSCs-CM and Apocynin on ROS production, HK-2 cells (7 × 10
4
/well) were seeded in 24-well plates. TGF-β1 was added and treated for 48 h, followed by continued treatment with different concentrations of Apocynin (50, 100, 200, 500, 1000 µM) for another 24 h for ROS probe labeling to observe the effect on ROS generation. Simultaneously, HK-2 cells (5,000/well) were seeded in 96-well plates, and CCK8 was used to detect the effect of different concentrations of Apocynin on cell viability. To compare the differences in ROS generation and the expression of the endogenous antioxidant stress signal nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) and the antioxidant enzyme CAT protein between MSCs-CM and Apocynin, HK-2 cells were seeded in 24-well plates (7 × 10
4
/well) or cell culture dishes (1.5 × 10
5
/well), and divided into 8 groups: Con, TGF-β1, TGF-β1 + MSCs-CM, TGF-β1 + Apocynin, TGF-β1 + MSCs-CM + Apocynin, MSCs-CM, Apocynin, and MSCs-CM + Apocynin. After TGF-β1 treatment, Apocynin (200 µM) or MSCs-CM or both were continued to treat the cells for 24 h. Cell samples were collected and proteins were extracted, and western blot was used to detect the expression of NRF2 and CAT proteins.
Mitochondrial biological activity assays
To observe the effect of MSCs-CM on the mitochondrial bioactivity of HK-2 cells, equal amounts of HK-2 cells were seeded in a 6-well plate, grouped, and treated similarly to the ROS detection without a positive control. Mitochondrial fluorescent probes were loaded following the Mito-Tracker Red CMXRos detection kit instructions (Beyotime, China). Under a 200× microscope, five different fields of fluorescent images were collected, and their grayscale values were analyzed using ImageJ software.
To preliminarily observe the effects of MSCs-CM on ARMC1 and oxidative stress resistance in the TGF-β1 induced HK-2 fibrosis model, the protein expression of ARMC1, mitochondrial fission protein (DRP1), and antioxidant stress capacity (Nrf2 and CAT) was detected by Western blot.
Construction of lentiviral vectors for ARMC1 gene regulation cells
To study the role of ARMC1 gene regulation in the antifibrotic process of MSCs, we utilized lentiviral vectors (Genechem, Shanghai, China) to knockdown and overexpress the Armc1 gene (ARMC1-KD and ARMC1-OE) in HK-2 cells, with an empty vector as controls (KD-Con and OE-Con). Western blot confirmed the expression of Armc1 protein. After the antibiotic screening, the four cell lines KD-Con, OE-Con, ARMC1-KD, and ARMC1-OE were continuously cultured under normal culture conditions for 24, 48, and 72 h, followed by CCK8 assay to detect cell viability.
Mitochondrial dynamics and oxidative stress resistance detection
Under the condition of ARMC1-OE, in order to study the effects of MSCs-CM on mitochondrial dynamics, biological activity, and antioxidant stress capacity of HK-2 cells treated with TGF-β1, cells were divided into two primary groups: the OE-Con group and the ARMC1-OE group. Each group was further divided into five subgroups, and the grouping and treatment of all subgroups were the same as the mitochondrial bioactivity detection. The protein expression of mitochondrial dynamics (ARMC1, DRP1, MFN1, MFN2, OPA1), oxidative stress resistance (NRF2, SOD1, SOD2, CAT), and fibrosis (α-SMA, FN, KIM-1) was detected by Western blot. Similarly, Mito-Tracker Red CMXRos was used to assess the mitochondrial bioactivity of cells in each group.
Cisplatin-induced renal interstitial fibrosis in mice, grouping and treatment
Cisplatin was a widely used chemotherapy drug with nephrotoxicity. Cisplatin caused an imbalance in the intracellular redox state, resulting in excessive ROS [
15
]. Both cisplatin and TGF-β1 can promote p53 phosphorylation and subsequent tubular dysfunction through NOXs-mediated ROS production [
17
]. Therefore, oxidative stress is one of the key factors promoting the process of renal fibrosis [
18
]. The kidneys are one of the organs with high oxygen consumption and are rich in mitochondria, especially in proximal tubular epithelial cells. The mechanism of adenine-induced renal fibrosis was that excessive adenine can be converted into adenosine monophosphate and adenosine triphosphate in the body, leading to the accumulation of metabolic alterations in the renal tubules, which may cause cytotoxicity, resulting in damage and death of renal tubular epithelial cells, as well as local inflammatory responses, affecting normal renal function [
19
]. So, the cisplatin-induced mouse model has become a classic model for studying the oxidative stress damage and fibrosis. Although the two modeling methods were different, both primarily exhibited renal interstitial fibrosis as the main pathological manifestation.
To observe whether the ARMC1 gene increases the anti-oxidative stress capacity to improve fibrosis by regulating dynamics in the MSCs anti-cisplatin induced renal interstitial fibrosis model, we chose male C57BL/6J mice as the research subjects. A total of 70 male C57BL/6J mice, aged 6 to 8 weeks (weight 20–30 g), were obtained from the Experimental Animal Center of Southwest Medical University. The mice were maintained in a controlled environment at 24 °C and 50% relative humidity, following a 12-hour light/dark cycle. They underwent various experiments in a specific pathogen-free (SPF) laboratory within the center. Throughout the study, all procedures complied with relevant animal ethics laws and regulations. The experiment received approval from Southwest Medical University, under the animal ethics number SWMU20240014. The work has been reported in line with the ARRIVE guidelines 2.0_Cisplatin.
C57BL/6J mice were randomly assigned to seven groups: the Control, the Cisplatin, the Cisplatin + MSCs group, the Cisplatin + Apocynin group, the C group, the Cisplatin + MSCs + Apocynin group, and the Cisplatin + MSCs + Mdivi-1 group, 10 mice per group. Mdivi-1(MCE, Shanghai, Chian) is a selective inhibitor of Drp1, which can effectively block the processes of mitochondrial fission and mitophagy, serving as a control for the effects on mitochondrial dynamics during the anti-cisplatin-induced fibrosis process of MSCs. Apocynin (MCE, Shanghai, China) is a selective NADPH oxidase inhibitor, used as a control against the oxidative stress damage. Mice were injected intraperitoneally with a saline solution of cisplatin at a concentration of 1 mg/mL (7 mg/kg) once a week for four consecutive weeks to create a model of cisplatin-induced nephropathy. Starting from the fifth week, the Cisplatin + Mdivi-1 group, Cisplatin + Apocynin group, Cisplatin + MSCs + Mdivi-1 group, and Cisplatin + MSCs + Apocynin group received Mdivi-1 or Apocynin intervention, with a concentration of 1 mg/mL and a standard of 10 mg/kg, administered by intraperitoneal injection once a day for 7 consecutive days. Simultaneously, the MSCs group, MSCs + Mdivi-1 group, and MSCs + Apocynin group received a tail vein injection of a cell density of 1 × 10
6
/mL MSCs suspension (1 × 10
7
/kg). The control group was given an equivalent volume of solvent. To adhere to animal ethics principles and ensure the welfare of the mice at the end of the experiment, we first anesthetized them intraperitoneally with a 1% pentobarbital sodium (50 mg/kg) and then performed euthanasia through cervical dislocation, ensuring that the mice ended their lives without pain at the conclusion of the sixth week. And then, the kidneys were harvested and weighed, and cardiac blood samples were collected.
Mouse kidney function testing
All mice were fasted the night before blood collection. Mice were anesthetized intraperitoneally with 1% pentobarbital sodium, and cardiac blood samples were collected via thoracotomy. Subsequently, serum was collected by centrifugation at 3500 rpm for 15 min to assess renal function indicators, specifically blood urea nitrogen and creatinine. The serum creatinine levels were determined using the creatinine oxidase method, while the serum urea nitrogen levels were assessed using the urease method according to the instructions of the test kit (Nanjing Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, Nanjing, China). Additionally, the kidney index was calculated using the formula: kidney weight divided by mouse weight, multiplied by 100%.
Mouse kidney pathological staining
The kidney tissue was fixed using 4% paraformaldehyde, followed by gradient alcohol dehydration, xylene infiltration, and then embedded in paraffin before sectioning to a thickness of 5 μm. For all groups, the kidney tissues underwent a standard process of xylene deparaffinization and gradient alcohol hydration. Subsequently, the sections were stained using Hematoxylin and Eosin (HE), Masson, and Red Sirius according to the reagent kit (Solarbio Biological Co., Ltd., Beijing, China). Once the staining was completed, images were captured using a light microscope. The tubular injury score was mainly based on the degree and extent of tubular injury, changes in renal tubular epithelial cell morphology, alterations in tubular lumen, and interstitial inflammation [
20
,
21
]. For each mouse, four to six high-power fields (HPF, 200×) of the same level were selected to assess collagen deposition and the integrated optical densities of immunohistochemically labeled collagen I and α-SMA. This evaluation was conducted semi-quantitatively using Image Pro Plus version 6.0 software (Media Cybernetics, Silver Spring, USA).
Western blot
The samples of cells were lysed on ice using RIPA lysis buffer supplemented with 1 mM PMSF (Beyotime, China), and the protein concentration was measured with a BCA kit (Beyotime, China). For kidney tissues, approximately 100 mg of tissue was collected and subsequently homogenized into a fine powder utilizing liquid nitrogen. The powder was subsequently transferred into a 1.5 mL tube, where 500 µL of RIPA lysis buffer was incorporated to promote effective lysis, while maintaining the mixture on ice to preserve protein integrity. Upon completion of the lysis procedure, the mixture was subjected to centrifugation at a velocity of 10, 000 rpm for a duration of 15 min at a temperature of 4 °C. Following centrifugation, the supernatant was extracted, and the protein concentration was also quantified using a BCA assay kit. For protein separation, 25–30 µg of protein was loaded onto an 8.0-12.5% SDS-PAGE gel, followed by transferring the proteins to a 0.45–0.22 μm PVDF membrane (Millipore, USA). After blocking the membrane with 5% skim milk, the following antibodies were incubated overnight at 4 °C: α-SMA (1:5000, Proteintech, USA), E-Cadherin (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), Collagen Type I (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), Fibronectin (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), KIM-1 (1:1000, SAB, USA), Bax (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), Bcl-2 (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), ARMC1 (1:1000, Invitrogen, USA), MFN1 (1:2000, Proteintech, USA), MFN2 (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), DRP1 (1:1000, Proteintech, USA), OPA1 (1:1000, Abcam, UK), NRF2 (1:2000, Abcam, UK), SOD1 (1:1000, Abcam, UK), SOD2 (1:1000, Abcam, UK), and CAT (1:1000, Abcam, UK). The PVDF membrane was then incubated with horseradish peroxidase (HRP) conjugated goat anti-rabbit or mouse secondary antibody for 2 h, followed by three washes with Tris Buffered Saline with Tween 20 (TBST). Afterward, the membrane was treated with a chemiluminescent HRP substrate (Beyotime, China), and the protein bands were visualized using the SH-Compact523 imaging system (Shenhua Technology, Hangzhou, China). Finally, the protein bands were quantified using Gel-Pro Analyzer software.
Statistical methods
In this study, all experimental results were expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) derived from a minimum of three biological replicates. Statistical analyses were conducted utilizing GraphPad Prism 9.0 software (San Diego, CA, USA). To assess group differences, one-way ANOVA or two-way ANOVA was applied, accompanied by Tukey post hoc tests. A p-value less than 0.05 was considered to indicate a significant statistical difference.
Results
MSCs improved kidney injury and function in adenine-induced nephropathy
HE staining revealed that adenine induced tubular dilation, localized infiltration of inflammatory cells, luminal crystal formation, moderate to severe dilation of the renal tubular lumen, with a large number of cellular debris present within the renal tubular lumen, and disorganized tissue architecture (Fig.
1
A). The kidney index of rats treated with adenine showed an obvious increase (Fig.
1
B), revealing typically enlarged white kidney (Fig.
1
J). Adenine significantly promoted the deposition of collagen constituents in the renal tissues, as evidenced by Sirus Red and Masson staining (Fig.
1

Intervention with MSCs notably reduced the kidney index, renal tubular injury, collagen deposition, and levels of Col-I and α-SMA proteins in the renal tissues, with big white kidney relief (Fig.
1

Proteins exhibiting a differential expression were defined as those showing a 1.2-fold change and a p-value of less than 0.05 between groups. Compared to the adenine group, MSC intervention resulted in significant differential expression of 40 proteins, of which 30 proteins were upregulated. Among them, the expression of ARMC1 protein showed the largest difference, increasing by 3.521 times (Fig.
2
A, red box, and Fig.
2
C). These differential expression protein-related GO terms and functional clusters were classified between the adenosine group and the adenosine + MSCs group (Fig.
2
B, D). The GO analysis showed that the protein ARMC1 (UniProt Accession: B0BN83), which had the highest upregulation fold during the process of MSCs against adenine-induced nephropathy rats, mainly participating in the binding of certain proteins or metal ions in the mitochondria or nucleus.

Discussion
Regardless of whether it is CKD or AKI, renal fibrosis is one of the significant pathological changes that cannot be ignored in kidney diseases. So far, anti-fibrosis treatment remains a research challenge. Currently, MSCs have shown unique therapeutic potential in the treatment of AKI or CKD, such as multifaceted potential, immune regulation function, secretion of various growth factors and cytokines, low immunogenicity, promotion of angiogenesis, different administration routes, and potential self-renewal capability [
22
–
24
], . The literature also clearly indicated that both MSCs and their derivatives had a good anti-fibrotic effect both in vivo and in vitro with good safety [
25
,
26
]. This study also demonstrated good anti-fibrotic effects of MSCs in both in vivo and in vitro experiments, but the anti-fibrosis mechanism still needs further research. In the adenine-induced nephropathy rat model, kidney proteomics indicated that MSCs significantly increased the expression of ARMC1 protein (Fig.
2
). According to the GeneCards databases (
https://www.genecards.org/
), ARMC1 is a subunit of the MICOS/MIB, mainly involves in regulating mitochondrial dynamics, playing a role in determining mitochondrial length, distribution, and movement. Mitochondria lacking ArmC1 did not have defects in cristae structure, respiration, and protein content, but exhibited fragmentation and reduced motility [
11
,
12
]. There is a close interrelationship between mitochondrial dynamics imbalance and oxidative stress damage, both of which play important roles in cellular physiological and pathological processes [
18
]. The dynamics of mitochondria mainly involve two processes, fission and fusion. These processes are crucial for maintaining the morphology, function, and overall health of mitochondria. Mitochondrial fission can remove damaged mitochondria and promote their renewal. It is mainly regulated by proteins such as dynamin-related protein 1 [
27
]. Excessive mitochondrial fission is often associated with an increase in oxidative stress [
28
]. High levels of ROS activated DRP1, promoting mitochondrial fission and leading to an increase in the number of mitochondria within the cell, but the functions of these mitochondria may be impaired. Mitochondrial fusion can help restore mitochondrial functions by mixing the contents of healthy and damaged mitochondria, reducing the production of ROS, and thereby alleviating oxidative stress [
18
]. It was mainly regulated by proteins such as MFN1, MFN2, and OPA1 [
29
]. Oxidative stress damage was one of the important mechanisms promoting the fibrosis process [
30
]. Subsequent studies should seek out renal fibrosis models that are closely related to oxidative stress damage. Therefore, the choice of cisplatin-induced renal fibrosis model is related to its modeling mechanism. Cisplatin was a widely used chemotherapy drug with renal toxicity, primarily for the treatment of various types of cancer. Cisplatin can enter renal tubular epithelial cells, causing an imbalance in intracellular redox status and generating a large amount of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These ROS can trigger cell damage, apoptosis, and necrosis [
15
]. Cisplatin can promote p53 phosphorylation and subsequent renal tubular dysfunction through ROS production mediated by NADPH oxidases (NOXs) [
17
]. Meanwhile, kidney is one of the organs with high oxygen consumption and are rich in mitochondria, especially the proximal renal tubular epithelial cells, which makes them a pathologically vulnerable site in kidney disease. Although literature showed that MSCs may increase mitochondrial quantity and quality in cancer by activating the AMPK pathway [
31
], it remains unclear whether MSCs can influence mitochondrial dynamics through the regulation of the ARMC1 gene in renal fibrosis. Based on the above description, we speculated that MSCs may influence mitochondrial dynamics balance and inhibit oxidative stress damage to alleviate renal fibrosis by regulating the ARMC1 gene. In vitro, the results revealed that TGF-β1 could inhibit ARMC1 protein expression with prolonged treatment time. MSCs-CM significantly upregulated ARMC1 protein expression, inhibited the expression of the key mitochondrial fission protein DRP1 (Fig.
4
). Perry and others revealed the critical role of blocking mitochondrial fission in maintaining mitochondrial function and preventing fibrosis progression after acute kidney injury through specific DRP1 knockout mice [
32
]. Mitochondrial fusion helped reduce the production of ROS, as fusion promoted metabolic balance and energy efficiency within the mitochondria. In contrast, excessive mitochondrial fission may lead to an increase in ROS, which can trigger oxidative stress and cell damage [
33
]. The mitochondrial dynamics changes caused by MSCs intervention may enhance mitochondrial bioactivity and strengthen the defense against oxidative stress damage, as MSCs can significantly increase the expression of NRF2 and CAT proteins (Fig.
4
). This was consistent with the literature on the activation of antioxidant stress signals by MSCs in a cisplatin-induced nephrotoxicity disease model [
34
]. Under the premise of ARMC1-OE, this trend was more pronounced at the cellular level, and the improvement in fibrosis was more significant (Fig.
5
). The overexpression of the ARMC1 gene in HK-2 cells may play a key role in improving the mitochondrial balance in damaged HK-2 cells, especially by inhibiting mitochondrial fission, increasing mitochondrial bioactivity and endogenous oxidative stress resistance. Although we are unclear how MSCs lead to increased expression of ARMC1 protein, MSCs exerted anti-fibrotic effects mainly by relying on the large amount of secreted cell factors [
35
], but it can be speculated that some cytokines secreted by MSCs act on the damaged HK-2 cells’ mitochondria. Due to the confounding of cytokines, it is difficult to clarify.
As is well known, the main source of ROS is mitochondria, and promoting mitochondrial balance to alleviate ROS oxidative stress damage is one of the important mechanisms to improve the fibrosis process. In the cisplatin-induced renal fibrosis model, NADPH oxidase-mediated ROS generation was another major source [
17
]. Therefore, we choose a selective NOX4 inhibitor Apocynin to inhibit ROS generation, rather than targeting the mitochondria. In the supplementary cell experiments, there was no significant difference in the inhibition of ROS generation and the effects on Nrf2 and CAT expression between MSCs and Apocynin, but the combination of the two showed a certain difference (Supplementary Fig. 2). Mdivi-1, a Drp1 inhibitor, directly inhibited mitochondrial fission. In kidney tissues, cisplatin led to an increase in the mitochondrial fission protein DRP1, while MSCs promoted the increase of ARMC1 protein and the decrease of DRP1 protein, indirectly reflecting the effect of increased ARMC1 expression on the inhibition of mitochondrial fission. And inhibiting DRP1 can also lead to an increase in ARMC1 protein. This operation is not as direct as conditionally overexpressing the ARMC1 gene in mouse kidney tissues. In vivo, Apocynin was less effective than the DRP1 inhibitor Mdivi-1, showing a certain difference between the two. Due to the strong paracrine effect of cytokines, MSCs not only inhibited the production of ROS but also promoted mitochondrial fusion, thereby enhancing mitochondrial bioactivity and the ability to resist oxidative stress damage. ARMC1-OE showed a positive effect in MSCs on inhibiting oxidative stress damage to improve renal fibrosis. In vivo experiments implied that inhibiting mitochondrial fission was probably more prominent in improving renal fibrosis than inhibiting ROS generation. Furthermore, solitary interventions yielded less effective compared to synergistic combinations. Notably, the simultaneous application of MSCs and Mdivi-1 has resulted in the most significant anti-fibrotic effects. This was particularly evident in the alterations of mitochondrial dynamics indicators, which significantly surpass those observed in the MSCs combined with Apocynin intervention group. MSCs significantly improved kidney function and renal pathology across three distinct intervention groups. MSCs may facilitate alterations in mitochondrial dynamics and enhance mitochondrial bioactivity, thereby helping to counteract damage caused by oxidative stress. From the perspective of anti-fibrotic characteristics, inhibiting the production of ROS wase less effective than enhancing mitochondrial dynamics. Numerous studies reported that improving mitochondrial dynamics can significantly enhance cellular functions in various ways, including reducing oxidative stress, optimizing energy metabolism, and promoting cell survival and growth. Furthermore, this process plays a role in reducing inflammation, promoting cell proliferation, and increasing the sensitivity of cells to external signals, ultimately influencing cellular behavior and offering a range of other benefits [
36
–
38
]. This study showed that MSCs may enhance antioxidant stress damage and delay renal fibrosis by upregulating ARMC1 gene expression, promoting mitochondrial fusion, and enhancing mitochondrial bioactivity. Mitochondria lacking ArmC1 demonstrated no abnormalities in cristae architecture, respiration, or protein composition, but did exhibit fragmentation and diminished motility [
12
]. In vitro, knocking out the ARMC1 gene in HK-2 cells resulted in a significant reduction in cell proliferation. Even when cells were cultured in standard medium with higher serum concentrations, they are facing difficulties in surviving. This might be attributed, to some extent, to the structure of the lentiviral vector. The significant decline in mitochondrial bioactivity alongside the obviously decreased proliferation of ARMC1-KD cells underscored the essential function of ARMC1 in maintaining normal mitochondrial operations and facilitating cellular growth. Of course, the precise influence of MSCs on ARMC1 expression remained ambiguous, and the underlying mechanism through which TGF-β1 suppressed ARMC1 expression was also yet to be elucidated. ARMC1 may play a crucial role in the regulation of mitochondrial dynamics markers such as DRP1, MFN1, MFN2, and OPA1, which influenced mitochondrial bioactivity. The precise mechanisms involved warrant further investigation, and there was a notable deficiency in ultrastructural studies concerning mitochondrial dynamics at the organelle level, necessitating additional evidence for validation.

Mitochondria are intricately linked to the emergence and progression of renal fibrosis [
2
]. These essential organelles within cells are pivotal for a multitude of crucial biological activities, including the generation of energy, regulation of metabolism to sustain cellular energy equilibrium and metabolic stability, storage and management of calcium ions, production and detoxification of reactive oxygen species, control of apoptosis, metabolic signaling, synthesis of specific biomolecules such as certain hormones, lipids, and amino acids, preservation of intracellular pH balance, and involvement in thermogenesis [
39
–
42
]. Mitochondrial damage and dysfunction significantly influenced the advancement of numerous diseases, with a plethora of studies establishing a strong correlation between mitochondrial dysfunction and diverse forms of AKI [
43
] and CKD [
44
]. Targeting mitochondria for therapeutic interventions has emerged as a prominent focal point in contemporary disease research [
45
]. Renal fibrosis frequently occurs alongside impairment of both the functionality and structure of renal parenchymal cells. The underlying mechanisms of fibrosis remain not entirely elucidated [
46
]. During renal fibrosis, the kidney, as one of the high-oxygen-consuming organs, may encounter detrimental environments such as oxidative stress and inflammation, leading to significant impairment of mitochondrial biological functions [
47
]. Fibrosis consequently resulted in an elevation of ROS production within the mitochondria, which in turn inflicted damage upon both the mitochondrial membrane and its DNA [
48
]. During the fibrosis process, cellular stress and apoptosis signals can trigger alterations in mitochondrial morphology. This often manifested as an imbalance between mitochondrial fission and fusion, leading to either swelling or fragmentation of the mitochondria. Such changes can significantly impair mitochondrial function, and contributed to the progression of fibrosis [
49
]. So, the kidneys exhibit significant metabolic activity with a high density of mitochondria, making the regulation of mitochondrial homeostasis during fibrosis a crucial strategy for antifibrotic treatment.
Our research indicated that a key antifibrotic mechanism of MSCs was the regulation of mitochondrial dynamics to promote mitochondrial homeostasis. However, the numerous cytokine secretion capabilities of MSCs make their anti-fibrosis mechanism complex, possibly involving multiple targets. We only conducted a preliminary verification in the mouse model of fibrosis induced by cisplatin. Whether this effect will also have a similar impact in the adenine-induced nephropathy or diabetic nephropathy or ischemia-reperfusion models requires further verification. From the perspective of mitochondrial dynamics, upregulation of ARMC1 inhibited mitochondrial fission and alleviated oxidative stress damage, which may be one of the important mechanisms by which MSCs resist renal fibrosis (Fig.
9
). Although this investigation did not elucidate the precise mechanism by which ARMC1 inhibited the crucial molecule DRP1, which was integral to the fission of the mitochondrial outer membrane, insighted gleaned from the STRING database suggest that ARMC1 may engage with a protein hypothesized to be instrumental in mitochondrial fission, referred to as mitochondrial fission regulator 1-like protein (MTFR1L). Further evidence is also required.
Conclusions
In summary, our findings indicated that MSCs could significantly mitigate renal fibrosis by modulating mitochondrial dynamics and oxidative stress via the enhancement of ARMC1 expression in cisplatin-treated mice and TGF-β1-induced HK-2 cells, presenting a promising avenue for the development of therapeutic interventions for renal fibrosis.
